title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
section: 2.2 Introducing ggplot2: Distribution of Students by Race
text:
2.2 Introducing ggplot2: Distribution of Students by Race
ggplot2 is an R package for declaratively creating data-driven graphics based on The Grammar of Graphics.
It is also part of the tidyverse family specially designed for visual exploration and communication.
For more detail, visit ggplot2 link.o(^_-)O

2.2.1 Basic Bar Chart Using geom_bar()
The first visualisation is a simple bar chart showing the distribution of students by race. Since RACE is a categorical variable, geom_bar() is suitable because it counts the number of observations in each category automatically.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) + 
  geom_bar(
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    width = 0.65
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Students by Race",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme










2.2.2 Improving the Bar Chart Design
The basic bar chart correctly shows the distribution of students by race, but the default ggplot2 style can be improved. The following version adds a clearer title, axis labels, a cleaner theme, and a more intentional colour design.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE, fill = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.35, width = 0.65) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = race_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Students by Race",
    subtitle = "Based on the Exam_data dataset",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








From the improved bar chart, Chinese students form the largest group in the dataset, followed by Malay students. Indian students and students classified under Others make up much smaller groups. This indicates that the dataset is not evenly distributed across race categories, which should be considered when interpreting later comparisons by race.


2.2.3 Aesthetic Mapping versus Fixed Aesthetic
In ggplot2, aesthetics can be controlled in two different ways. If an aesthetic such as fill is placed inside aes(), it is mapped to a variable in the dataset. If it is placed outside aes(), it is applied as a fixed visual setting.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    width = 0.65
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Students by Race with Fixed Fill Colour",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme








Unlike the previous improved bar chart, this version uses a fixed fill colour. The colour is not linked to the RACE variable, so all bars share the same colour. This is useful when the purpose is to compare bar heights without using colour to represent categories.


2.2.4 Comparing geom_bar() and geom_col()
geom_bar() is used when the dataset contains raw observations and ggplot2 needs to count the number of rows in each category. In contrast, geom_col() is used when the dataset already contains summarised values.

race_count <- exam_data %>%
  count(RACE)

race_count

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  RACE        n
  <chr>   <int>
1 Chinese   193
2 Indian     12
3 Malay     108
4 Others      9


The summarised table can now be visualised using geom_col(). Unlike geom_bar(), geom_col() does not count rows automatically. Instead, it uses the pre-calculated n column as the height of each bar.

ggplot(data = race_count,
       aes(x = RACE, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2A6F6F", color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.35, width = 0.65) +
  labs(
    title = "Race Distribution Using Summarised Data",
    subtitle = "Using geom_col() with pre-counted values",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








This bar chart is created using geom_col(), which is suitable when the dataset has already been summarised. In this case, the table race_count contains the pre-calculated number of students in each race category, and the column n is mapped to the y-axis. Unlike geom_bar(), geom_col() does not perform automatic counting.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
section: 2.3 Visualising the Distribution of English Scores
text:
2.3 Visualising the Distribution of English Scores
After examining the distribution of a categorical variable, the next step is to explore a numerical variable. In this section, the English scores are visualised to understand the overall score distribution, including the spread, concentration, and possible unusual values.

2.3.1 Dot Plot of English Scores
A dot plot gives a compact view of how individual English scores are distributed. Each dot represents observations around a score value, making it useful for seeing where the scores are clustered.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_dotplot(
    binwidth = 2.5,
    dotsize = 0.6,
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Dot Plot of English Scores",
    subtitle = "Each dot represents students grouped by similar score values",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )










2.3.2 Histogram of English Scores
The histogram shows the overall distribution of English scores more clearly than the dot plot. Most students are concentrated in the middle score ranges, while very low and very high scores appear less frequently.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#5B7F6E",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Histogram of English Scores",
    subtitle = "Distribution of English scores in 5-point intervals",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








English scores cluster mainly between 60 and 80, with the strongest concentration around the 70s. The thinner bars at both ends suggest that very low and near-perfect scores are relatively uncommon.


2.3.3 Modifying geom_histogram()
The appearance of a histogram can be adjusted by changing the arguments inside geom_histogram(). Here, the bin width is made wider so that the score distribution is grouped into broader intervals.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 10,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#D95F02",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Distribution with Wider Bins",
    subtitle = "Using 10-point intervals",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








With wider bins, the histogram looks less detailed but shows the overall shape of the score distribution more clearly.


2.3.4 Modifying Aesthetic Mapping
Aesthetic mapping changes how variables are connected to visual features. In this histogram, GENDER is mapped to fill, so the bars show how English score distributions differ between male and female students.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.3,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = gender_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Distribution by Gender",
    subtitle = "Using fill mapping inside aes()",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )








Mapping `GENDER` to `fill` adds a second layer of information to the histogram. The bars are now coloured by gender, making it easier to see how male and female students contribute to the overall English score distribution.


2.3.5 Density Plot of English Scores
A density plot provides a smoother view of the score distribution. It is useful when the goal is to see the general shape of the data without focusing on individual histogram bins.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_density(
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Density Plot of English Scores",
    subtitle = "A smoother view of the score distribution",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








The curve peaks around the higher-middle score range, which is consistent with the histogram pattern. Compared with the histogram, the density plot gives a cleaner view of the overall shape.


2.3.6 Boxplot of English Scores by Gender
A boxplot is useful for comparing the distribution of a numerical variable across groups. Here, English scores are compared between male and female students.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = GENDER, y = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.8,
    outlier.color = "#D95F02",
    outlier.size = 2
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = gender_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "English Scores by Gender",
    subtitle = "Comparing median, spread, and possible outliers",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "English Score",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








The boxplot makes the gender comparison more compact than the histogram. It highlights the median score, the spread of scores, and any possible outliers in each group.


2.3.7 Violin Plot of English Scores by Gender
Boxplots are compact, but they can feel a little too compressed. A violin plot opens up the shape of the distribution, making it easier to see where scores are packed more tightly.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = GENDER, y = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_violin(
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.75,
    trim = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    fill = "white",
    alpha = 0.7,
    outlier.color = "#D95F02",
    outlier.size = 1.8
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = gender_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Shape by Gender",
    subtitle = "Violin plot with a compact boxplot overlay",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "English Score",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








The violin shape makes the score pattern less flat than a boxplot. The wider sections mark where more students are clustered, while the narrow tails show thinner score ranges.


2.3.8 Scatter Plot of Maths and English Scores
A scatter plot is useful when the question shifts from “how one variable is distributed” to “how two variables move together”. Here, each point represents one student, with Maths score on the x-axis and English score on the y-axis.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Maths and English Scores",
    subtitle = "Each point represents one student",
    x = "Maths Score",
    y = "English Score"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








The point cloud leans clearly upward: stronger Maths scores usually come with stronger English scores. There are a few scattered exceptions, but the overall relationship is hard to miss.


2.3.9 Adding a Trend Line to the Scatter Plot
The scatter plot already hints at a positive relationship. Adding a smooth trend line makes that pattern easier to read, especially when there are many points on the chart.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.55,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    color = "#D95F02",
    fill = "#F2A65A",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Maths and English Scores with Trend Line",
    subtitle = "Linear trend added using geom_smooth()",
    x = "Maths Score",
    y = "English Score"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








The fitted line cuts cleanly through the point cloud, reinforcing the positive relationship between Maths and English scores. The shaded band gives a quick sense of uncertainty around the trend.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.4 Working with Statistical Summaries
So far, the charts have mostly shown raw observations. Statistical summaries go one level higher: instead of plotting every individual value, they calculate a summary value first, then display it.

2.4.1 Mean English Score by Gender

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = GENDER, y = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "bar",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.8,
    width = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = gender_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean English Score by Gender",
    subtitle = "Using stat_summary() to calculate group means",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Mean English Score",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








Instead of showing every English score, this chart compresses each gender group into one mean value. It is cleaner, but also more ruthless: the spread and outliers disappear, so the chart should be read together with the earlier boxplot.


2.4.2 Mean English Score with Error Bars
A mean bar alone looks clean, but it hides too much. Error bars add a quick check on how stable the mean comparison is.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = GENDER, y = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "bar",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.8,
    width = 0.6
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.18,
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = gender_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean English Score by Gender with Error Bars",
    subtitle = "Bars show means; error bars show standard error",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Mean English Score",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








The bars still show the average English score for each gender, but the error bars stop the chart from pretending the averages are perfectly fixed. It is a small addition, but it makes the comparison more honest.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.5 Faceting
Faceting splits one chart into smaller panels. Instead of squeezing every group into one plot, it gives each group its own little stage.

2.5.1 English Score Distribution by Class

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ CLASS) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Distribution by Class",
    subtitle = "Each panel shows one class",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








Faceting makes class-level patterns easier to scan. Instead of mixing all students into one histogram, each class gets its own panel, so differences in spread and concentration are easier to spot.


2.5.2 Faceting by Gender and Race
facet_grid() arranges panels like a grid. This is useful when two categorical variables are involved and the comparison needs a cleaner structure.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#D95F02",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  facet_grid(GENDER ~ RACE) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Distribution by Gender and Race",
    subtitle = "Rows show gender; columns show race",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








The grid layout is stricter than facet_wrap(): gender runs down the rows, while race runs across the columns. Some panels are sparse, which is a useful reminder that subgroup comparisons can get fragile when the sample size becomes small.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.6 Coordinates
Coordinate settings change how a plot is displayed without changing the underlying data. A simple example is flipping the x-axis and y-axis to make a bar chart easier to read.

2.6.1 Flipping the Bar Chart

ggplot(data = race_count,
       aes(x = RACE, y = n)) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    width = 0.65
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Race Distribution with Flipped Coordinates",
    subtitle = "Same data, different reading direction",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








Flipping the chart does not change the counts. It simply turns the bars sideways, which makes category labels easier to read and gives the chart a cleaner rhythm.


2.6.2 Zooming into the Score Range
Sometimes the full axis range is not the most useful view. Here, the plot is zoomed into the main score range so the dense middle section is easier to inspect.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(40, 100),
    ylim = c(40, 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Zoomed View of Maths and English Scores",
    subtitle = "Using coord_cartesian() to focus on the main score range",
    x = "Maths Score",
    y = "English Score"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )








This zoomed view keeps the original data intact but focuses the display on the main score band. It is cleaner for reading the dense area, without pretending the lower scores never existed.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.7 Working with Themes
Themes control the non-data parts of a chart: background, grid lines, title style, axis text, legend position, and spacing. A good theme should not fight for attention; it should make the data easier to read.

2.7.1 Applying a Custom Theme

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    color = "#D95F02",
    fill = "#F2A65A",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Maths and English Scores with a Custom Theme",
    subtitle = "Theme settings improve readability without changing the data",
    x = "Maths Score",
    y = "English Score"
  ) +
  vaa_chart_theme +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.25, color = "grey85")
  )








The theme changes do not alter the data or the statistical relationship. They simply clean up the visual surface: less noise, clearer text, and a chart that feels more intentional.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.8 Summary
This exercise shows how ggplot2 builds charts layer by layer. The same dataset can be explored from different angles: categorical distributions with bar charts, score distributions with dot plots, histograms and density plots, group comparisons with boxplots and violin plots, and score relationships with scatter plots.
The main takeaway is that ggplot2 is not just about drawing charts. It is about deciding what each layer does: what data to use, what variables to map, what geometric object to choose, what statistical summary to calculate, how to split panels with facets, how to adjust coordinates, and how to refine the final look with themes.

title: Hands-on_Ex09b
text:
Point maps are used when each observation has a coordinate pair. Unlike choropleth maps, the unit of analysis is a location rather than an area. Symbol size, colour and shape can then be used to encode additional attributes.
In this hands-on exercise, Singapore Pools outlet data is converted from an aspatial table into an sf point layer. The points are mapped over Singapore subzones and then redesigned as proportional symbol maps.
By the end of this exercise, we should be able to:

import point data with projected coordinates;
convert a data frame into an sf point object;
draw point symbol maps;
draw proportional symbol maps;
compare point patterns by outlet type;
use a base polygon layer to provide geographic context.





if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pacman", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}

pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  sf,
  scales,
  knitr
)






The point data file is SGPools_svy21.csv. It includes outlet names, addresses, coordinates, outlet type and the Gp1Gp2 Winnings field used for proportional symbols.
A Singapore subzone shapefile is also included in this exercise folder so the points can be mapped on a recognisable base map.

pools_path <- "data/aspatial/SGPools_svy21.csv"
sg_path <- "data/geospatial/MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL.shp"

if (!file.exists(pools_path) || !file.exists(sg_path)) {
  stop("The Singapore Pools CSV or Singapore subzone shapefile is missing.")
}

sg_map <- st_read(sg_path, quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_make_valid()

sgpools <- read_csv(pools_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(sgpools)

Faceting gives each outlet type its own panel. This reduces overlap and makes the spatial pattern of each group easier to inspect.

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = sg_map, fill = "grey94", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  geom_sf(

    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),

Equal-sized point maps are good for checking location, while proportional symbols add magnitude.
Symbol size and colour should not compete; each should encode a clear variable.
A summary table is helpful when overlapping circles make exact comparison difficult.

title: Hands-on_Ex09c
text:
Analytical mapping goes beyond displaying a single count. It uses derived measures, classification rules and outlier logic to support comparison across areas.
In this hands-on exercise, Nigerian water point data is used to map non-functional water points. The exercise starts with a count map, then moves to rate maps, percentile maps and box maps.
By the end of this exercise, we should be able to:

import a prepared sf object from an RDS file;
derive functional and non-functional rates;
map counts and rates;
build percentile classes;
create a box-map classification based on the interquartile range;
identify areas that are unusually high or low.





if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pacman", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}

  tidyverse,
  sf,
  scales,

Percentile mapping highlights values at the tails of a distribution. The classes below separate the bottom 1 percent, bottom 10 percent, middle range, top 10 percent and top 1 percent.

nga_percentile <- nga_rate %>%
  mutate(
    pct_rank_nonfunctional = percent_rank(pct_nonfunctional),
    percentile_class = case_when(
      is.na(pct_rank_nonfunctional) ~ NA_character_,
      pct_rank_nonfunctional <= 0.01 ~ "Bottom 1%",
      pct_rank_nonfunctional <= 0.10 ~ "Bottom 10%",
      pct_rank_nonfunctional < 0.90 ~ "Middle 80%",
      pct_rank_nonfunctional < 0.99 ~ "Top 10%",
      TRUE ~ "Top 1%"
    ),
    percentile_class = factor(
      percentile_class,
      levels = c("Bottom 1%", "Bottom 10%", "Middle 80%", "Top 10%", "Top 1%")
    )
  )


ggplot(nga_percentile) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = percentile_class), colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Bottom 1%" = "#2A6F6F",
      "Bottom 10%" = "#A8DADC",
      "Middle 80%" = "grey88",
      "Top 10%" = "#F2A65A",
      "Top 1%" = "#D95F02"
    ),
    na.value = "grey95"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Percentile Map of Non-functional Water Point Rate",
    fill = "Class"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )











A box map applies the logic of a boxplot to a map. It highlights areas beyond the interquartile range as possible spatial outliers.

rate_values <- nga_rate$pct_nonfunctional
q1 <- quantile(rate_values, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
q2 <- quantile(rate_values, 0.50, na.rm = TRUE)
q3 <- quantile(rate_values, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
iqr_value <- q3 - q1
lower_fence <- q1 - 1.5 * iqr_value
upper_fence <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr_value

nga_box <- nga_rate %>%
  mutate(
    box_class = case_when(
      is.na(pct_nonfunctional) ~ NA_character_,
      pct_nonfunctional < lower_fence ~ "Low outlier",
      pct_nonfunctional < q1 ~ "Lower quartile",
      pct_nonfunctional < q2 ~ "Below median",
      pct_nonfunctional < q3 ~ "Above median",
      pct_nonfunctional <= upper_fence ~ "Upper quartile",
      TRUE ~ "High outlier"
    ),
    box_class = factor(
      box_class,
      levels = c(
        "Low outlier",
        "Lower quartile",
        "Below median",
        "Above median",
        "Upper quartile",
        "High outlier"
      )
    )
  )


ggplot(nga_box) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = box_class), colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.05) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Low outlier" = "#7570B3",
      "Lower quartile" = "#A8DADC",
      "Below median" = "#F7FBFF",
      "Above median" = "#F2A65A",
      "Upper quartile" = "#D95F02",
      "High outlier" = "#1F1F1F"
    ),
    na.value = "grey95"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Box Map of Non-functional Water Point Rate",
    subtitle = "High outliers are above Q3 plus 1.5 times the IQR",
    fill = "Box-map class"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )












Rate maps can exaggerate small denominators. The scatterplot below checks whether high non-functional rates are attached to areas with very few total water points.

nga_rate %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(total_wp > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(total_wp, pct_nonfunctional)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, colour = "#2A6F6F") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "#D95F02") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Checking Rate Stability",
    subtitle = "Small denominators can create very high or very low rates",
    x = "Total water points, log scale",
    y = "Non-functional rate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))












Count maps and rate maps answer different questions.
Percentile maps are useful for highlighting distribution tails.
Box maps apply outlier logic to spatial data.
Denominators matter: a high rate in a very small area should be interpreted carefully.

title: ISS608-VAA
text:
Cover


Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility


ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1 · Visual Analytics for Data Discovery


Cheng Yuanyuan · 23 May 2026



This executive summary uses the same motor insurance portfolio data, but applies a different visual analytics path from the earlier version. The focus is on distribution, concentration, pricing adequacy, and exposure-adjusted segment comparison. The slide deck is designed to support management decisions rather than only describe variables.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Observation 1 — The dataset is large enough for exposure-adjusted portfolio analysis
text:
Observation 1 — The dataset is large enough for exposure-adjusted portfolio analysis



The portfolio contains 354,140 policy-year records and 185,678 insured IDs.
Exposure is explicitly available, so comparisons should be made using premium/exposure, claims/exposure, and incurred/exposure, not raw totals alone.
Implication: the dataset supports credible portfolio-level visual analytics, provided segment comparisons are exposure-adjusted.



This slide checks whether the data structure supports the assignment purpose. The key issue is that policy records do not all represent identical exposure. Therefore, the analysis uses exposure-weighted measures. The missingness plot is included because variables with high missingness should not be used for strong causal claims without caution.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Analytical Framework — Separate volume, price, frequency, severity and tail risk
text:
Analytical Framework — Separate volume, price, frequency, severity and tail risk


Pricing adequacyPortfolio loss ratio = incurred / premium. This is the main profitability metric.


Claim frequencyClaims / exposure identifies how often adverse events occur.


Claim severityIncurred / claim separates expensive claims from frequent claims.




Exposure baseExposure prevents small segments from being overinterpreted.


Tail volatilityECDF and Pareto views reveal concentration not visible in averages.


ValidationTests and model diagnostics check whether visual differences persist statistically.



The analysis deliberately avoids treating average loss ratio as a sufficient answer. Insurance profitability is skewed, zero-heavy, and segment-dependent.


The framework follows an actuarial logic. Loss ratio explains premium adequacy, but it does not tell whether the problem comes from claim frequency or severity. Exposure matters because small groups can look extreme simply by chance. The selected methods therefore combine distribution plots, concentration analysis, segment charts, heatmaps, and statistical checks.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Observation 2 — Premium and incurred cost move differently over time
text:
Observation 2 — Premium and incurred cost move differently over time



Indexed trends show whether premium rate, incurred cost, claim frequency, and loss ratio move together or diverge.
Implication: if incurred cost rises faster than premium rate, portfolio growth is not automatically profitable.



This chart is chosen instead of four separate bar charts because indexing allows direct comparison of metrics with different units. It shows whether premium, claims, and loss ratio are moving in the same direction. For management, the key point is the relative movement, not the raw accounting totals.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Observation 3 — Loss experience is zero-heavy and strongly right-skewed
text:
Observation 3 — Loss experience is zero-heavy and strongly right-skewed



ECDFs are more suitable than normal curves because most policy-years have no claims or no incurred loss.
Implication: averages alone are unstable; later segment comparisons should use capped distributions and portfolio-weighted summaries.



This slide uses ECDFs because they show the full cumulative distribution without assuming normality. Histograms would be dominated by the spike near zero, while ECDFs still show the long right tail. The zero-share bar makes the zero-heavy structure explicit.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 1 — A small tail of policy-years contributes a large share of incurred losses
text:
Insight 1 — A small tail of policy-years contributes a large share of incurred losses



The Pareto curve shows whether losses are broadly distributed or concentrated in a small adverse tail.
Implication: volatility management should focus on tail exposure, not only average segment performance.



A Pareto curve is used because insurance losses are often concentrated. This view is more decision-useful than a single mean or median because it tells management whether most losses come from many ordinary policies or a small tail of severe outcomes.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 2 — Premium level does not fully explain incurred loss
text:
Insight 2 — Premium level does not fully explain incurred loss



The binned density view avoids overplotting hundreds of thousands of policy-years.
Implication: pricing review should look for clusters above the break-even line, where incurred loss exceeds premium.



A normal scatterplot would be unreadable because the dataset is large. A binned heatmap preserves the relationship between premium and incurred loss while showing where records are concentrated. The dashed line provides an intuitive profitability reference.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 3 — Product type remains a primary profitability separator
text:
Insight 3 — Product type remains a primary profitability separator



Product comparisons use portfolio-weighted loss ratio and exposure share together.
Implication: a high loss ratio is more urgent when the product also carries meaningful exposure.



A lollipop plot is used instead of a bar chart to emphasise relative ranking without visually overloading the slide. Exposure share is shown beside the loss ratio because management should not treat a tiny product and a large product as equally important.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 4 — Bonus score separates risk, but distributions overlap
text:
Insight 4 — Bonus score separates risk, but distributions overlap



Violin + boxplot shows both distribution shape and median/IQR, rather than hiding overlap behind one average.
Implication: bonus score is useful, but it should be combined with other underwriting variables.



This chart was selected because a pure bar chart would imply each bonus group is homogeneous. The violin layer shows distribution spread, while the boxplot gives a familiar summary. The paired claim-frequency chart helps separate how often claims happen from how large the resulting losses are.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 5 — Payment and business context change risk mix
text:
Insight 5 — Payment and business context change risk mix



The heatmap shows combined effects rather than evaluating payment frequency alone.
Implication: payment behaviour should be interpreted together with business context before repricing.



A two-way heatmap is selected because payment frequency and business type may interact. This is better than separate one-variable bar charts, which can hide combined risk pockets. The line chart then shows whether differences are driven by claim frequency.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 6 — Vehicle brand outliers require exposure-aware screening
text:
Insight 6 — Vehicle brand outliers require exposure-aware screening



Funnel plot avoids overreacting to small brands with unstable loss ratios.
Implication: brands above the exposure-adjusted band deserve deeper underwriting review.



This chart is chosen because brand groups have unequal exposure. A simple ranked bar chart would overstate small-exposure outliers. A funnel plot is more defensible because it compares segment loss ratio against exposure-adjusted tolerance bands.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 7 — Vehicle value and power create interaction-based risk pockets
text:
Insight 7 — Vehicle value and power create interaction-based risk pockets



Interaction heatmap shows risk pockets that one-variable charts cannot identify.
Implication: vehicle pricing should monitor combinations, not only independent variables.



The heatmap is selected because the management question is about combinations of characteristics. Vehicle value or power alone may not reveal the highest-risk cells. Filtering out low-exposure cells avoids giving too much attention to unstable small groups.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Method Add-on — Distribution shapes differ by product and bonus group
text:
Method Add-on — Distribution shapes differ by product and bonus group



Density and quantile-profile views expose distribution shape, not only central tendency.
Implication: the best pricing signal is not only which group has the highest mean, but which group has a thicker adverse tail.



This is the advanced visual analytics add-on. It uses distribution-shape diagnostics rather than another simple bar chart. The density chart compares product-level shape, while the quantile profile shows how groups diverge across the distribution, including the upper tail.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Statistical Validation — Visual differences are checked formally
text:
Statistical Validation — Visual differences are checked formally



Non-parametric validation is used because capped loss ratio is still skewed and non-normal.
Implication: visual findings are not presented as decoration; they are checked against statistical evidence.



The Kruskal-Wallis test is used because the outcome distribution is skewed and has many zeros. The purpose is not to replace visual analytics, but to check whether the visual segment differences are statistically visible. A claim-occurrence chart adds a frequency-side validation.

title: ISS608-VAA
text:
Final Recommendations

1. Price by exposure-adjusted loss ratio, not raw incurred totals.Loss ratio is the main portfolio profitability metric, but it must be interpreted with exposure.


2. Separate frequency risk from severity risk.High claim frequency and high incurred severity point to different underwriting actions.


3. Prioritise product and bonus-score review.These variables create visible profitability separation and should enter the first pricing shortlist.


4. Use funnel screening before acting on small segments.Extreme loss ratios in low-exposure brands can be noise; funnel plots provide a more defensible signal.


5. Monitor interaction pockets.Vehicle value × power-to-weight combinations reveal risk pockets that single-variable summaries can miss.


Overall conclusion: profitability pressure is not random. It is concentrated in observable product, bonus, payment, vehicle, and brand-risk structures. The next step should be actuarial modelling, but the visual analytics already identifies where management attention should begin.


The recommendations translate the visual analysis into decision rules. The strongest practical conclusion is that management should not use one overall loss ratio alone. It should separate pricing adequacy, frequency, severity, exposure size, and interaction pockets before repricing or underwriting intervention.

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
This report investigates the premature release of embargoed Project HarborCrest merger information in VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1. Based on the communication logs, the breach appears more consistent with a system-level communication control failure than a clearly coordinated deliberate leak.
The evidence shows three major patterns. First, communication volume increased substantially in later simulation rounds, indicating escalation and coordination pressure. Second, embargo-related keywords such as HarborCrest, merger, embargo, FleX, Judge, and public release terms became concentrated in later rounds. Third, high-risk messages were not evenly distributed across all agents; they were concentrated among specific roles and channels.
The main implication is that the breach was likely enabled by repeated exposure to sensitive information and weak containment between internal deliberation and outward-facing communication channels. The data shows involvement and exposure, but it does not provide enough evidence to prove malicious intent.


Code
json_candidates <- c(
  "data/mc1/MC1_final_00.json",
  "data/MC1_final_00.json",
  "data/VAST_Challenge_2026_MC1/MC1_final_00.json"
)

json_path <- json_candidates[file.exists(json_candidates)][1]

if (is.na(json_path)) {
  stop(
    "MC1_final_00.json not found. Put it in data/mc1/MC1_final_00.json, ",
    "data/MC1_final_00.json, or data/VAST_Challenge_2026_MC1/MC1_final_00.json."
  )
}

mc1_raw <- fromJSON(json_path, simplifyVector = FALSE)

if (!"rounds" %in% names(mc1_raw)) {
  stop("The JSON file does not contain a 'rounds' object.")
}

rounds <- purrr::imap_dfr(mc1_raw$rounds, function(round, i) {
  tibble(
    round_id = i,
    round_hour = ymd_hms(round$hour),
    event_headline = round$environment_context$event_headline %||% NA_character_,
    event_narrative = round$environment_context$event_narrative %||% NA_character_,
    social_state = round$environment_context$social_state %||% NA_character_
  )
})

communications_df <- purrr::imap_dfr(mc1_raw$rounds, function(round, i) {
  purrr::map_dfr(round$communications %||% list(), function(comm) {
    tibble(
      round_id = i,
      round_hour = ymd_hms(round$hour),
      message_id = comm$message_id %||% NA_character_,
      agent_id = comm$agent_id %||% NA_character_,
      agent_role = comm$agent_role %||% NA_character_,
      agent_label = comm$agent_label %||% NA_character_,
      channel = comm$channel %||% NA_character_,
      message_type = comm$message_type %||% NA_character_,
      responding_to = comm$responding_to %||% NA_character_,
      timestamp = ymd_hms(comm$timestamp),
      content = comm$content %||% NA_character_,
      reacting = comm$internal_state$reacting %||% NA_character_,
      rationalizing = comm$internal_state$rationalizing %||% NA_character_,
      deliberating = comm$internal_state$deliberating %||% NA_character_
    )
  })
}) %>%
  mutate(
    content = if_else(is.na(content), "", content),
    agent_role = if_else(is.na(agent_role) | agent_role == "", "Unknown", agent_role),
    agent_label = if_else(is.na(agent_label) | agent_label == "", agent_id, agent_label),
    channel = if_else(is.na(channel) | channel == "", "Unknown", channel),
    text_all = str_squish(paste(content, reacting, rationalizing, deliberating, sep = " ")),
    phase = case_when(
      timestamp < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 09:00:00") ~ "Pre-crisis baseline",
      timestamp < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:25:00") ~ "Crisis before release",
      timestamp < ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00") ~ "Pre-embargo release cascade",
      TRUE ~ "Post-embargo response"
    ),
    phase = factor(
      phase,
      levels = c(
        "Pre-crisis baseline",
        "Crisis before release",
        "Pre-embargo release cascade",
        "Post-embargo response"
      )
    )
  )

required_comm_cols <- c(
  "round_id", "round_hour", "message_id", "agent_id", "agent_role",
  "agent_label", "channel", "message_type", "content", "timestamp"
)

missing_comm_cols <- setdiff(required_comm_cols, names(communications_df))

if (length(missing_comm_cols) > 0) {
  stop(paste("Missing expected columns in communications_df:", paste(missing_comm_cols, collapse = ", ")))
}

risk_pattern <- regex(
  "harborcrest|civicloom|tenantthread|merger|embargo|flex|announcement|leak|judge|public|broadcast|social",
  ignore_case = TRUE
)

deal_pattern <- regex("civicloom|harborcrest|merger", ignore_case = TRUE)

release_posts <- communications_df %>%
  filter(
    phase == "Pre-embargo release cascade",
    message_type == "public_post",
    str_detect(content, deal_pattern)
  )

if (nrow(release_posts) == 0) {
  stop("No pre-embargo release posts were found. Check phase boundaries and message_type values.")
}

first_release_time <- min(release_posts$timestamp)
last_release_time <- max(release_posts$timestamp)
release_post_count <- nrow(release_posts)
release_agents <- release_posts %>%
  count(agent_label, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(agent_label, " (", n, ")")) %>%
  pull(label) %>%
  paste(collapse = ", ")

pre_crisis_public_deal_posts <- communications_df %>%
  filter(
    phase == "Pre-crisis baseline",
    message_type == "public_post",
    str_detect(content, deal_pattern)
  ) %>%
  nrow()

crisis_before_public_deal_posts <- communications_df %>%
  filter(
    phase == "Crisis before release",
    message_type == "public_post",
    str_detect(content, deal_pattern)
  ) %>%
  nrow()

signal_events <- tibble(
  message_id = c(
    "20460605_14_008",
    "20460605_14_021",
    "20460605_18_001",
    "20460605_19_001",
    "20460605_20_001",
    "20460605_21_026"
  ),
  signal = c(
    "PR-Intern hears 'CivicLoom timeline at 6 PM'",
    "PR identifies an active containment problem",
    "The Judge monitors a critical environment",
    "The Judge issues a maximum-threshold warning",
    "Intern posts a personal signal during the critical window",
    "Legal publishes first pre-embargo merger confirmation"
  )
) %>%
  left_join(communications_df, by = "message_id") %>%
  mutate(
    evidence = str_trunc(content, 190),
    signal = factor(signal, levels = rev(signal))
  )

if (any(is.na(signal_events$timestamp))) {
  stop("One or more expected signal message IDs were not found in the dataset.")
}

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
2 Data Preparation
The original MC1 dataset is stored as a nested JSON file. The top-level object contains 23 simulation rounds. Each round includes the simulation hour, environment context, communication records, and participant information.
For this analysis, the communication records were extracted from the nested JSON structure and converted into a flat analytical table. Each message was linked back to its simulation round and round timestamp. The final communication table contains agent identifiers, agent roles, channels, message types, message content, and timestamps.
This preparation step is important because the investigation depends on comparing communication intensity, agent behaviour, channel usage, and embargo-related message content across rounds. Keeping the wrangling process inside the Quarto document also improves reproducibility, because the figures are generated directly from the raw MC1 JSON file.

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
section: 3 Direct Breach Evidence and Event Sequence
text:
3 Direct Breach Evidence and Event Sequence
The Mini-Challenge 1 brief asks for key events, relationships, decision points, and actors involved in the inappropriate release. The most important finding is that the breach was not just a general increase in risky language. It was a specific pre-embargo public-release cascade.
The first explicit public post mentioning CivicLoom, HarborCrest, or the merger appears at 05:25 PM on June 5, 2046. The last pre-embargo deal post in the cascade appears at 05:54 PM. Across this window, 7 public posts used deal-specific language before the 6:00 PM embargo lift. These posts came from Legal-Agent (4), Social-Manager-Agent (3).

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
4 Typical Versus Release Behaviour
The release behaviour was new because deal-specific public posting was absent in normal baseline activity and then appeared repeatedly in the 35-minute pre-embargo cascade. This comparison is more precise than overall message volume alone because it separates routine communication from public posts containing CivicLoom, HarborCrest, or merger language.


Code
phase_release_comparison <- communications_df %>%
  mutate(
    public_deal_post = message_type == "public_post" & str_detect(content, deal_pattern),
    actor_group = case_when(
      agent_id == "legal_agent" ~ "Legal-Agent",
      agent_id == "social_media_agent" ~ "Social-Manager-Agent",
      TRUE ~ "Other agents"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(public_deal_post) %>%
  count(phase, actor_group, name = "public_deal_posts")

ggplot(phase_release_comparison, aes(x = phase, y = public_deal_posts, fill = actor_group)) +
  geom_col(color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.35) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Legal-Agent" = "#2A6F6F",
      "Social-Manager-Agent" = "#8AA6A3",
      "Other agents" = "#BFBFBF"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Public Deal Posts Were Concentrated in the Release Cascade",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Baseline public deal posts: ", pre_crisis_public_deal_posts,
      "; crisis-before-release public deal posts: ", crisis_before_public_deal_posts,
      "; release-cascade public deal posts: ", release_post_count, "."
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = "Public posts containing deal terms",
    fill = "Actor group"
  ) +
  theme_mc1() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 18, hjust = 1))








Figure 2: Typical behaviour compared with the pre-embargo release cascade.





This chart directly answers the normal-versus-release requirement. Earlier activity may contain high-risk internal discussion, but the release behaviour was the public posting of deal-specific terms by Legal and Social-Manager agents before the embargo lifted.

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
5 Communication Intensity Across Simulation Rounds
The first step is to identify when communication activity intensified. A sudden increase in message volume can indicate escalation, coordination pressure, or decision-making around the embargoed information.


Code
communication_volume <- communications_df %>%
  count(round_id, round_hour, name = "message_count") %>%
  arrange(round_id)

ggplot(communication_volume, aes(x = round_id, y = message_count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2A6F6F", color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_text(aes(label = message_count), vjust = -0.35, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = communication_volume$round_id) +
  labs(
    title = "Communication Volume Across Simulation Rounds",
    subtitle = "Message count by round in the MC1 communication log",
    x = "Simulation Round",
    y = "Number of Messages"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )








Figure 3: Communication volume across simulation rounds.





The chart shows that communication activity increased substantially in the later rounds, especially around Rounds 15–17 and 20–22. These spikes suggest that the breach did not emerge from a single isolated message, but from a period of intensified communication and coordination. ## Agent Roles Involved in the Communication Chain
After identifying when communication intensified, the next step is to examine which agent roles contributed most to the communication flow. This helps identify the actors most involved in the information chain before the embargo breach.


Code
role_volume <- communications_df %>%
  count(agent_role, name = "message_count") %>%
  arrange(desc(message_count))

ggplot(role_volume, aes(x = reorder(agent_role, message_count), y = message_count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2A6F6F", color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_text(aes(label = message_count), hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Communication Volume by Agent Role",
    subtitle = "Total number of messages contributed by each agent role",
    x = "Agent Role",
    y = "Number of Messages"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )








Figure 4: Communication volume by agent role.





The chart shows which agent roles were most active in the simulation. Roles with higher message volume are more likely to have shaped the communication environment in which the embargo breach developed. This does not prove intent, but it identifies the main participants that require closer examination.

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
6 Embargo-related Keyword Mentions Across Rounds
To identify possible leading indicators, this section tracks messages that mention terms related to the embargoed Project HarborCrest information. A rise in these terms before the breach may indicate that sensitive information was already circulating through the agent communication system.


Code
keyword_pattern <- regex(
  "harborcrest|civicloom|tenantthread|merger|embargo|flex|announcement|leak|judge|public",
  ignore_case = TRUE
)

keyword_trend <- communications_df %>%
  mutate(
    content_clean = if_else(is.na(content), "", content),
    keyword_flag = str_detect(content_clean, keyword_pattern)
  ) %>%
  group_by(round_id, round_hour) %>%
  summarise(
    total_messages = n(),
    keyword_messages = sum(keyword_flag, na.rm = TRUE),
    keyword_share = keyword_messages / total_messages,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(round_id)

ggplot(keyword_trend, aes(x = round_id, y = keyword_messages)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2A6F6F", color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_text(aes(label = keyword_messages), vjust = -0.35, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = keyword_trend$round_id) +
  labs(
    title = "Embargo-related Keyword Mentions Across Rounds",
    subtitle = "Messages mentioning HarborCrest, CivicLoom, merger, embargo, FleX, Judge, or public release terms",
    x = "Simulation Round",
    y = "Number of Keyword-related Messages"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )








Figure 5: Embargo-related keyword mentions across simulation rounds.





The chart shows a clear increase in embargo-related language in the later simulation rounds. This provides evidence of leading indicators: sensitive terms were appearing repeatedly before the final breach point, suggesting that the system was already operating in a high-risk communication state.

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
7 Channel Usage Across Simulation Rounds
The next step is to examine how messages moved through different communication channels. This is important because an embargo breach depends not only on what was said, but also on where the information was transmitted.


Code
channel_usage <- communications_df %>%
  count(round_id, round_hour, channel, name = "message_count") %>%
  arrange(round_id, desc(message_count))

ggplot(channel_usage, aes(x = round_id, y = message_count, fill = channel)) +
  geom_col(color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(channel_usage$round_id))) +
  labs(
    title = "Channel Usage Across Simulation Rounds",
    subtitle = "Distribution of messages by communication channel in each round",
    x = "Simulation Round",
    y = "Number of Messages",
    fill = "Channel"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )








Figure 6: Channel usage across simulation rounds.





The chart shows how communication channels were used across the simulation. A concentration of activity in broad or outward-facing channels would indicate that sensitive information had greater opportunity to move beyond controlled internal discussion.

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
8 Agent Role and Channel Usage
To understand how different agents participated in the communication system, this heatmap compares agent roles against communication channels. This helps identify whether sensitive or outward-facing channels were mainly used by particular types of agents.

  count(agent_role, channel, name = "message_count") %>%
  arrange(desc(message_count))

Figure 7: Agent role and channel usage heatmap.





The heatmap shows how communication activity was distributed across agent roles and channels. This is useful for identifying whether specific agent roles were associated with channels that could amplify or expose sensitive information.

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
9 High-risk Message Evidence
The previous charts show aggregate patterns. To support the investigation with direct evidence, this section extracts messages containing terms related to the embargo, Project HarborCrest, FleX, public release, and system control.

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
12 Findings
The visual evidence suggests that the embargo breach was not caused by a single isolated message. Communication volume increased noticeably in the later simulation rounds, especially around the same period where embargo-related keywords also became more frequent. This indicates that the system entered a higher-risk communication state before the final breach.
The agent-role analysis shows that sensitive communication was concentrated among specific roles rather than evenly distributed across all participants. In particular, legal and social-media-related roles appeared prominently in high-risk messages. This does not prove intentional leakage by those roles, but it shows that they were important nodes in the sensitive information flow.
The channel-based analysis also matters. An embargo failure requires both sensitive content and a pathway through which that content can move. The channel visualisations suggest that communication structure, not just message content, contributed to the risk. Once sensitive information appeared repeatedly across roles and channels, the probability of accidental exposure increased.
Overall, the strongest evidence points to escalating system pressure followed by an executable release cascade. The breach was enabled by system-level control failure, but the final public posts were coherent, repeated, and actor-specific rather than random noise.

title: Investigating the TenantThread Embargo Breach
text:
13 Response to Mini-Challenge 1 Questions

13.1 Question 1: What were the key events, relationships, decision points, and actors involved?
The breach developed through a sequence of escalating communication rounds rather than through one isolated message. The key event chain was: early exposure to the “CivicLoom timeline at 6 PM” phrase, PR recognition of a containment problem, a maximum-threshold Judge warning, and then public merger-specific posts beginning at 05:25 PM.
The most important actors were Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent, who produced the pre-embargo public deal posts. PR and PR-Intern were important earlier in the chain because they surfaced and interpreted warning signals. The main decision-point failure was that The Judge’s warning did not translate into a hard publishing block before 6:00 PM.


13.2 Question 2: How did breach-related behaviour differ from normal behaviour?
The later rounds showed higher communication intensity and more frequent use of embargo-related language. More importantly, public deal-term posting changed from 0 posts in the baseline phase to 7 posts during the pre-embargo release cascade. This differs from earlier rounds, where high-risk terms were more often internal signals or crisis discussion rather than public merger disclosure.
The difference was not only about message volume. The release behaviour combined actor concentration, public channels, and repeated deal-specific content. That combination made the breach behavior qualitatively different from normal communication.


13.3 Question 3: Were there leading indicators before the breach?
Yes. The clearest leading indicators were the 10:07 AM exposure of the CivicLoom/6 PM phrase, PR’s 10:20 AM containment concern, The Judge’s 3:00 PM maximum-threshold warning, the increase in embargo-related keyword mentions, and the concentration of high-risk messages among specific roles. These indicators appeared before the 5:25 PM public release and should have triggered stronger controls.
The evidence suggests that earlier warning signs were present but not effectively escalated. Repeated mentions of HarborCrest, merger, embargo, FleX, Judge, and public-release terms created a visible risk pattern. A stronger monitoring system should have treated these repeated signals as an embargo incident and blocked public posting until the official 6:00 PM release time.
